concept.text: A proof that no three positive integers a, b and c satisfy a^n + b^n = c^n for any integer n greater than 2. Proved by Andrew Wiles, with Richard Taylor, in 1995. Sources given: https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/ ; https://world-of-mathematics.com/blog/millennium-problems-overview/.

page.title: Proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem
page.definition: A proof that aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no solutions in positive integers a, b and c for any integer n>2. Andrew Wiles established the theorem in 1995, using a companion paper written with Richard Taylor.

goal.need: The goal concerns all positive integer triples and infinitely many integer exponents n>2. On 27 June 1908, Göttingen’s Royal Society of Sciences offered 100,000 marks for a resolution. The proof introduced methods used in the 2001 proof of modularity for all elliptic curves over the rational numbers.

completion.title: A proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem is peer-reviewed and published in Annals of Mathematics.
completion.criterion: A proof establishes that aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no solutions in positive integers a, b, c for any integer n>2 and is published after peer review in Annals of Mathematics, together with the companion arguments required to establish it.
completion.set_by: Refereed publication in Annals of Mathematics.
completion.threshold_quote: In particular, this finally yields a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.
completion.basis: The published proof consists of Andrew Wiles, “Modular elliptic curves and Fermat's Last Theorem”, Annals of Mathematics 141(3), 443–551 (1995), doi:10.2307/2118559, together with Richard Taylor and Andrew Wiles, “Ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras”, 141(3), 553–572 (1995), doi:10.2307/2118560. Peer review and publication in the Annals constitute confirmation of the proof. Wiles received the Wolfskehl Prize in 1997.

milestones.title: The equation x⁴ + y⁴ = u² is proved to have no positive integer solutions.
milestones.criterion: A proof excludes every positive integer triple (x,y,u) satisfying x⁴ + y⁴ = u². Substituting u=z² establishes Fermat’s Last Theorem for exponent 4. Fermat’s infinite-descent argument proves this stronger statement; the Abel Prize’s 2016 exposition reproduces the argument.
milestones.set_by: Mathematical community convention: Fermat’s infinite-descent theorem, reproduced with proof by Arne B. Sletsjøe for the Abel Prize.
milestones.threshold_quote: has no solution among the positive integers.

milestones.title: Modularity of semistable elliptic curves over Q is proved to imply Fermat’s Last Theorem.
milestones.criterion: A proof shows that a hypothetical Fermat counterexample with prime exponent p≥5 yields a semistable elliptic curve over the rational numbers Q that cannot be modular. Ribet’s level-lowering argument establishes this implication. Together with the known exponent 3 and exponent 4 cases, it reduces Fermat’s Last Theorem to modularity of semistable elliptic curves. Ribet proved the result in 1986 and published it in 1990.
milestones.set_by: Mathematical community convention: Kenneth Ribet, Corollary 1.2 and its proof in Inventiones mathematicae. The quoted corollary assumes modularity of all elliptic curves; its proof uses only semistable curves.
milestones.threshold_quote: Assume that all elliptic curves over Q are modular. Then Fermat’s Last Theorem is true.

milestones.title: Every semistable elliptic curve over the rational numbers is proved to be modular.
milestones.criterion: Every elliptic curve over Q—a smooth projective genus-one curve with a rational point—with good or multiplicative reduction at every prime admits a nonconstant map defined over Q from a modular curve X₀(N), for some positive integer N. The reduction condition defines semistability; the existence of the map defines modularity. Wiles’s Theorem 0.4 establishes this result in 1995 using Taylor and Wiles’s companion paper.
milestones.set_by: Mathematical community convention: the semistable case of the Shimura–Taniyama modularity conjecture, established as Theorem 0.4 in Wiles’s 1995 paper.
milestones.threshold_quote: Suppose that E is a semistable elliptic curve defined over Q. Then E is modular.

results.finding: Infinite descent excludes all positive integer triples (x,y,u) satisfying x⁴ + y⁴ = u², establishing Fermat’s Last Theorem for exponent 4.
results.detail: The source supplies the descent proof: a solution with minimal u would yield another with d < u, a contradiction. Peer review or proof-assistant verification is not stated.
results.quote:
An assumption that leads to a contradiction
can not be true, thus we have proved that
there can not exist any positive integer solu-
tion to the Fermat equation
x4 + y4 = u2

results.finding: All semistable elliptic curves over Q are proved modular in Theorem 0.4; the result is universal, with no finite sample.
results.detail: The proof uses the companion arguments in [TW]. Modularity is defined through a covering by X₀(N).
results.quote:
Theorem 0.4. Suppose thatE is a semistable elliptic curve deﬁned over
Q. ThenE is modular.

results.finding: Fermat’s Last Theorem is proved for every integer exponent n>2, excluding all positive integer solutions, in Annals of Mathematics (1995).
results.detail: Theorem 0.5 follows from the paper’s semistable modularity theorem and Ribet’s prior result; the required companion argument is credited to [TW].
results.quote:
Theorem 0.5. Suppose thatup +vp +wp =0 with u,v,w ∈ Q and p ≥ 3,
then uvw =0 . (Equivalently - there are no nonzero integersa,b,c,n with n> 2
such thatan + bn = cn.)

results.finding: Every elliptic curve over Q is proved modular, including every semistable elliptic curve; the result covers all curves, with no finite sample.
results.detail: Theorem 2.2.2 proves the stronger result without a semistability restriction, building on Wiles, Taylor–Wiles and earlier modularity results.
results.quote: Theorem 2.2.2. Every elliptic curve deﬁned over the rational numbers is modular.

results.finding: The formal proof excludes all nonzero integer solutions of a⁴ + b⁴ = c² with coprime a,b and odd a: 0 solutions.
results.detail: The machine-checked square-right-hand-side lemma requires coprimality and odd a. The unrestricted theorem proved afterward concerns x⁴ + y⁴ = z⁴; the text does not formalize the reduction of every positive integer solution with an arbitrary square right-hand side.
results.quote:
private lemma no-rewritten-fermat4:
¬ (∃ (a::int) b. (a^4 + b^4 = c^2∧ a∗b∗c⁄= 0∧ odd a ∧ coprime a b ))

results.finding: For all hypothetical Fermat counterexamples with prime exponent p≥5, level lowering forces the associated semistable curve’s representation to level 2, where no cusp forms exist.
results.detail: Theorem 5.1 and its application prove the implication: the counterexample curve has square-free conductor, and repeated level lowering contradicts the zero-dimensional space at level 2. The article supplies a modified proof of the author’s result.
results.quote:
This theorem immediately gives:
Conjecture of Taniyama-Shimura ==~ Fermat’s Last Theorem.

results.finding: Lean proves that x⁴ + y⁴ = u² has 0 positive integer solutions, covering every positive integer triple.
results.detail: The formal theorem excludes all integer triples with x and y nonzero, which includes every positive integer triple.
